en: Homage to the illustrious Nairātmyā! To that which they call the Dharmakāya, free from conceptual construction, and the beautiful Sambhogakāya, consisting of nothing but incomparable bliss;
May that Blessed One, Vajrasattva, whose emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) exists for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world, grant you prosperity.

In this single work, we shall clearly set forth, according to our understanding and in accordance with the scriptures, a concise and extensive treatise on the proof of selflessness that has been spread out [in other works].

Indeed, the yogi, dwelling in a place favorable to the mind such as a cremation ground, partaking of the commitments (*samaya*) of the five nectars and so forth, seated in a comfortable posture, free from attachment and fear, with a mind intent on the welfare of sentient beings, should generate the ego-identity of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and meditate on a blue syllable *HŪṂ* upon a sun disk at his heart.

Then, having drawn him forth by means of those blazing rays illuminating the triple world, [he visualizes himself as] the one residing in the Akaniṣṭha realm, surrounded by eight yoginīs, possessing sixteen arms and eight faces, with a crest fashioned from a garland of skulls, treading upon the four Māras with his four feet, blue in color, and holding in his multitude of right hands a skull-cup containing an elephant, a horse, a donkey, a bull, a camel, a human, a śarabha, and a jackal, all dissolved within it.

One should meditate upon him in front of oneself: holding a lotus vessel in his other hand, possessing the faces of Varuṇa, Samīraṇa, Jvalana, Rajanīnātha, Taraṇi, Yama, and Dhanada; with a principal face that is Kṛṣṇa (black), a right face as white as the moon or a jasmine flower, a left face exceedingly red, and an upper face extremely smoky and formidable; with all faces except one being very dark; adorned with a garland of fifty severed heads; with his neck embraced by Nairātmyā; and dwelling in the midst of the sky.

Immediately after that, one should perform worship with the eight yoginīs through the outer and secret worship of reality (*tattva*). And herein, for the sake of realizing the identity (*tādātmya*) of wisdom and means, there is the worship of Picu-vajra.

Then, having performed prostrations, the confession of sins, the vow of non-commission of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the going for refuge in the Three Jewels, the generation of the bodhicitta, the offering of one’s own body, and the request [to teach], and having cultivated the four Brahma-abodes, one should abide in a non-abiding form while contemplating the meaning of the mantra: "Oṃ! I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness; all phenomena are of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness," which consists of the essence that summarizes the reality of all things.

Then, recollecting his former vow, he arises from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Having visualized a sun disk in front of him by means of the syllable *repha* (ra), and having visualized a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) there by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, he should then contemplate a vajra-fortress, a binding canopy, a ground made of vajras below, and a moat, all formed by vajras that emanate from the crossed-vajra as a collection of atoms. Furthermore, by means of the sun and the crossed-vajra becoming rays of light and spreading out in all directions, he should solidify all of that.

Immediately after that, one should visualize in the space-element (*khadhātu*) the Wisdom (*prajñā*), which has the form of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), is hollow within, exceedingly thick and white, and is oriented upwards. Then, one should meditate upon a vast eight-petaled lotus of variegated colors situated within it. Then, in its center, one should contemplate a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from the transformation of the syllable *HŪṂ*, which rests in the middle of a sun-maṇḍala arisen from the syllable *RA*.

In the center of the universal vajra, one should visualize, one above the other, the elements of air, fire, water, and earth—smoky gray, red, white, and green—shaped like a bow, a triangle, a circle, and a square, respectively, and transformed from the syllables *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *laṃ*. Imagining all of this as mere consciousness, one should visualize the palace (*kūṭāgāra*) produced by that transformation: square, with four doors, adorned with eight pillars, and decorated with hanging garlands and half-garlands.

Then, one should visualize eight cremation grounds within the enclosure wall. Here, in the east, on a *harītakī* tree, is Devendra, dark blue in color and having the face of an elephant. In the south, on a mango tree, is Yama, white in color and having the face of a buffalo. In the west, on an *aśoka* tree, is Varuṇa, red and having the face of a lion. In the north, on a Bodhi tree, is Kubera, greenish-yellow in color and having the face of a human. In the southeast, on a *karañja* tree, is Vaiśvānara, white in color and having the face of a goat.

In the southwest, upon a *latājapā* flower, Naravāhana is pale and has a human face. In the northwest, upon a *kakubha* tree, Pavana is yellow and has the face of a deer. In the northeast, upon a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*), Bhūteśa is variegated and has the face of a bull. All of these hold a skull in their left hands, have their right hands occupied with various weapons, and display the upper halves of their bodies.

Thus, in the eight directions starting from the east, one should visualize, in due order, Ananta, Padma, Vāsuki, Mahāpadma, Takṣaka, Śaṅkhapāla, Karkoṭaka, and Kulika. One should also visualize eight clouds, possessing the colors black, white, pale-white, red, yellow, green, and variegated. Likewise, the eight guardians of the directions are to be understood as having their well-known colors. Furthermore, the eight *caityas* should be understood as having colors corresponding to their respective wings.

Then, having visualized a red eight-petaled lotus in the center of the mandala, one should behold fifteen corpses upon the four petals of that lotus in the east and other directions, as well as in the four corners of the gabled pavilion, at the four gates, and below and above. Immediately thereafter, one should meditate on the fifteen vowels beginning with *a*, situated between a moon and a sun disk produced from the *āli* and *kāli* [vowel and consonant] series, mounted upon those corpses. Then, through the transformation of the seed-syllables beginning with *a*, there is a curved knife (*kartī*) accompanied by its seed-syllable in every instance.

Then, through the transformation of the moon, the sun, and the seed-syllable along with the flaying knife (*kartikā*), one should meditate upon the fifteen yoginīs, beginning with Nairātmyā. In this context, the moon possesses the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); the sun possesses the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); the seed-syllable situated between them is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); the unification of all these is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*); and the perfection of the image is the utterly pure sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*).

Here, in the center of the lotus, one should meditate on Nairātmyā, who arises from the vowel *a*, whose nature is hatred, who is sealed by Akṣobhya, whose essence is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), and whose form is wisdom and method; her neck is embraced by a khaṭvāṅga representing external method. On the petals in the east and other directions, one should meditate on Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, and Vajraḍākinī, who arise from the vowels *ā, ī, u, ū*, whose natures are delusion, malice, passion, and envy, who are sealed by Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, and whose essences are the aggregates of form, sensation, perception, and mental formations.

Then, in the outer enclosure, one should visualize Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī in the corners starting from the northeast; they are produced from the vowels ū, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ, are sealed by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, and Amitābha, and have the nature of earth, water, fire, and air respectively.

Then, at the eastern and other gates, one should visualize Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī, who arise from the vowels *ḷ*, *ai*, *au*, and *aḥ*, are sealed with the mudrās of the consonants (the *sparśa* class), and have the nature of form, sound, smell, and taste. Immediately after that, below and above, one should visualize Bhūcarī and Khecarī, who arise from the vowels *au* and *aṃ*, are sealed with the mudrās of Delusion (*moha*) and Passion (*rāga*), have the intrinsic nature of the element of touch (*sparśadhātu*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and have the nature of cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, here, immediately after the generation of the goddesses, when the consecration by their respective family lords (*kuleśa*) occurs, the mudrās of their respective family lords are to be understood.

These fifteen yoginīs are sixteen years of age, situated within the solar mandala, with a luster like crushed collyrium; they are of the nature of bodhicitta, with flaming tawny hair standing erect. At the palate, they hold skull-cups four finger-breadths in size, which are of the nature of Vajrasattva. Upon their heads, they bear five skulls that are pure and of the nature of the five Buddhas. They have red, round, three-eyed faces with fangs bared in a terrifying mien, and are adorned with garlands of fifteen dry skulls of the nature of the fifteen Mātṛkās. Their waists and hips are draped in tiger skins.

Standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture, mounted upon corpses, and bearing the five mudrās; therein—Akṣobhya exists in the form of a wheel, Amitābha as earrings, Ratneśa in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana resides in the hand. (1)
Amoghasiddhi is situated on the girdle, and likewise Vajradhara on all the limbs;
the wheel on the head is for bowing to the Guru, the Ācārya, and the chosen deity.
One should wear earrings on the ears so as not to hear ill-spoken words from the Guru or the Vajradhara, and a necklace for the purpose of reciting mantras. (3)
Mekhala resolved to adopt the mudrā; Rucaka, to abandon the killing of living beings;
and Kṛṣṇāṅga, wearing anklets and armlets, [resolved to do so] through a mind of loving-kindness.

The blood-red tawny color of the hair is for the purpose of manifesting great passion (*mahārāga*); its upward direction is for the purpose of demonstrating wrath. Because body, speech, and mind have the nature of supreme passion, the eyes are by their very nature characterized by great passion. The two arms represent the natures of cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvana. The flaying knife is for the purpose of cutting away defects such as pride. Through the purification of the three realms, the skull—divided into three sections—is filled with the blood of the four Māras, namely the aggregates and so forth, and it is the body of all conceptual constructions. Through the purification of the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies, there are the three bends (*tribhaṅga*).

The slender body [is indicated] by the purity of the svābhāvikakāya. Wearing a tiger skin is for the purpose of proclaiming non-obstruction. Treading upon the sky with a single foot is for the purpose of proclaiming the lack of objective support (*anālambanatā*) regarding the three realms. Standing on the ground with one foot is for the purpose of proclaiming the state of having a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

Immediately thereafter, one should bring forth the wheel of Nairātmyā, whose nature is the Jñānasattva residing in the realm of Akaniṣṭha, by means of five-colored rays of light emerging from the seed-syllable located in the heart; having brought it forth, one should cause it to enter the seed-syllable in the heart. Having become one with the Jñānasattva and the Samayasattva, and maintaining the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of being Nairātmyā, one should become equal to Nairātmyā.

Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the practice of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), one should meditate on [the deities] in sequence with colors that are black, red, yellow, green, blue, and white.

In that regard, through the process of the intensification of cultivation, first [the object] appears like the full moon shrouded by clouds; from further intensification than that, it appears like an illusion; from further intensification than that, it manifests like a dream. Immediately thereafter, through the ripening of that intensification, the practitioner of Mahāmudrā attains non-differentiation between the states of dreaming and waking and achieves accomplishment. This is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

Apart from the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, the bodhicitta arises in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) situated between the supreme joy (*paramānanda*) and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*). One should instantly perceive that very [bodhicitta], which consists of fifteen digits (*kalā*), as having the form of the fifteen yoginīs with their previously mentioned colors, signs, and postures; for it possesses the nature of the five aggregates, the four elements, the six objects, and body, speech, and mind—this is the profound generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Alternatively, without even looking at the seed-syllable, one should instantly perceive the mandala-circle consisting of the fifteen yoginīs—this is the completion stage (*utpannakrama*).

Now, the stage of completion (*pariniṣpannakrama*). Indeed, when the vajra-body is empowered by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) flow from the place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). These are the fifteen yoginīs; thus, the body itself consists of the wheel of Nairātmyā. For instance, starting from the throat down to the navel, the *lalanā* and *rasanā* reside on the left and right sides and are known as the Moon and the Sun. Below the navel, those same two, the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, are the channels of the womb that carry blood and [semen] unshaken (*akṣobhya*).
The *avadhūtī* resides in the middle of the head, throat, heart, navel, and womb, and carries the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). These channels are Nairātmyā.

In the indestructible (*abhedyā*) and subtle channels located at the head and the crest-lock, which respectively carry the pair of characteristics of nails and teeth, and hair and body-hair, there is *Vajrā*. In the right ear, the divine (*divyā*) channel carries its own impurities; in the left, on the spinal column, the channel *Gaurī* carries flesh. In the left ear and between the eyebrows, belonging to Vāmanī and Kūrmajā, the channel *Vārī* carries the chains of sinews and bones. In the eyes and the roots of the arms, where Bhāvakī and Sekā reside, *Ḍākinī* carries the kidneys and the heart. In the armpits and breasts, where Doṣāvatī and Mahāviṣṭā reside, *Pukkasī* carries the eyes and bile.

Mātārī resides in both nostrils and carries the lungs and the intestinal chain; Śavarī resides in the cold and hot [channels] located in the mouth and throat, and carries the lateral ligaments and the abdomen; Caṇḍālī resides in the heart and carries excrement; and Ḍombī resides in the middle of the sīmantam at the penis and has a joyful countenance.

In the *svarūpiṇī*sāmānya, the two channels carrying phlegm (*śleṣman*) and bile (*pitta*) located at the penis and anus are Gaurī. In the state of separation from the *hetu*, the two channels carrying blood (*śoṇita*) and sweat (*sveda*) located in the thighs and shanks are Caurī. In the *premaṇī*siddha, the two channels carrying fat (*medas*) and tears (*aśru*) located in the big toe and the back of the foot are Vettālī. The two channels located in the big toe and the two knees belong to Pāvakī and Sumanā; among them, the former carries mucus (*kheṭa*) and the latter carries nasal mucus (*siṃhāṇa*). These are the Ghasmarīs.

In the petals of the heart-lotus, starting from the east and proceeding in order, are Trivṛttā, Ākāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, Māradārikā, and so forth. Among them, the first pair of channels is Bhūcarī; [the remaining ones are Khecarī]. Furthermore, whichever channel produces, nourishes, or moves toward a particular [element], it is designated as its "carrier" (vāhā).

Furthermore, these [deities], whose nature consists of the three realms of body, speech, mind, enjoyment, and emanation, are established within the four wheels (*cakra*) of the body. Among them, the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*) is multicolored, has sixty-four petals, possesses the black seed-syllable *A*, and is situated below the navel facing upward. The dharma wheel (*dharmacakra*) is a white eight-petaled lotus with the black seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, situated at the region of the heart. At the throat is the enjoyment wheel (*sambhogacakra*), which is red with sixteen petals and the red seed-syllable *Praṇava* (*OṂ*).

At the head is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), a white thirty-two-petaled lotus with a downward-facing white seed-syllable *haṃ*, dripping streams of nectar. Here, the distinctions between the moments of bliss (*ānandakṣaṇabheda*) and so forth are to be understood through the instruction of the guru.
The direct realization of the bodhicitta that flows as the non-dual union of effortless spontaneity (*anābhogayuganaddha*) is the natural sequence (*svābhāvikaḥ kramaḥ*).

Then, weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra while maintaining the ego-identity of selflessness (*nairātmyāhaṃkāra*). In this regard, the mantras consist of the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *svāhā*, which are fifteen in number and are by nature spontaneously accomplished (*sahajasiddha*). They are as follows: oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ svāhā. Maintaining the ego-identity of the red Nairātmyā, one should recite this mantra: oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā.
oṃ the letter *a* is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning; oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—this is the *bali* mantra.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ—the mantra for the empowerment of the commitment (samayādhiṣṭhāna).

Immediately thereafter, in the state of directly perceiving the maṇḍala circle, having taken hold of the breasts, one should place the *bola* situated within the *kakkola* of one's own consort. One should apply the bell to both sides.
Having understood the essence of the treatises in the Mantra Vehicle with effort from a true guru, [one should practice].
Out of compassion, we have composed this elucidation of selflessness.
Alas, how could there be for embodied beings here a definitive understanding of the wheel of the circle of the forest?
Unless their heads were not made rough by the pollen of the lotus feet of the Lord of the Śavaras.

Whatever merit may be acquired by this through the extensive [treatises on] the clear realizations, may the entire world have its self established in the state of the Vajra-holder, with the suffering and mental distress of the three realms destroyed.
The *Nairātmyāprakāśa*, as obtained within the *Abhisamayālaṅkāravistara*, is completed.
This work is by the venerable scholar and master, the feet of the illustrious Avadhūtādvayavajra.
